units.evidence: I think I'd have an easier time with Malick's metaphysical speculations if I had a sense of some concomitant geopolitical ones--central to any larger musings on forces of nature as viewed through the prism of war. Couldn't it be that the German and Japanese fascist orders were profoundly anti-natural, and that the Allies' cause was part of a violent but natural correction? You don't have to buy into Spielberg's Lincolnesque pieties in Saving Private Ryan to believe that there's a difference between World War II and Vietnam (or, for that matter, World War II and the invasion of Grenada or our spats with Iraq). While he was at Harvard, Malick might have peeled himself off the lap of his pointy-headed mentor, Stanley Cavell, the philosopher and film theorist, and checked out a few of Michael Waltzer's lectures on just and unjust wars. Maybe then he'd view Guadalcanal not in an absurdist vacuum (the soldiers come, they kill and are killed, they leave) but in the larger context of a war that was among the most rational (in its aims, if not its methods) fought in the last several centuries. For all his visionary filmmaking, Malick's Zen neutrality sometimes seems like a cultivated--and pretentious--brand of fatuousness.

units.claim: Rikud sobbed, 'Where's the buzzer? I must find the buzzer.'
units.evidence: Rikud, too, felt a strange light-headedness and a gnawing hurt in his stomach. But it didn't matter. He heard the angry voices and the feet pounding behind him, and he wanted only to get away. It was dark and he was hungry and everyone who was strong enough to run was chasing him, but every time he thought of the garden outside, and how big it was, the darkness and the hunger and the people chasing him were unimportant. It was so big that it would swallow him up completely and positively. He became sickly giddy thinking about it. But if he didn't open the door and go into the garden outside, he would die because he had no food and no water and his stomach gurgled and grumbled and hurt. And everyone was chasing him. He stumbled through the darkness and felt his way back to the library, through the inner door and into the room with the voice—but the voice didn't speak this time—through its door and into the place of machinery. Behind him, he could hear the voices at the first door, and he thought for a moment that no one would come after him. But he heard Crifer yell something, and then feet pounding in the passage. Rikud tripped over something and sprawled awkwardly across the floor. He felt a sharp hurt in his head, and when he reached up to touch it with his hands there in the darkness, his fingers came away wet. He got up slowly and opened the next door. The voices behind him were closer now. Light streamed in through the viewport. After the darkness, it frightened Rikud and it made his eyes smart, and he could hear those behind him retreating to a safe distance. But their voices were not far away, and he knew they would come after him because they wanted to break him. Rikud looked out upon the garden and he trembled. Out there was life. The garden stretched off in unthinkable immensity to the cluster of low mounds against the bright blue which roofed the many plants. If plants could live out there as they did within the world, then so could people. Rikud and his people should. This was why the world had moved across the darkness and the stars for all Rikud's lifetime and more. But he was afraid. He reached up and grasped the handle of the door and he saw that his fingers were red with the wetness which had come from his hurt head. Slowly he slipped to the cool floor—how his head was burning!—and for a long time he lay there, thinking he would never rise again. Inside he heard the voices again, and soon a foot and then another pounded on the metal of the passage. He heard Crifer's voice louder than the rest: 'There is Rikud on the floor!' Tugging at the handle of the door, Rikud pulled himself upright. Something small and brown scurried across the other side of the viewport and Rikud imagined it turned to look at him with two hideous red eyes. Rikud screamed and hurtled back through the corridor, and his face was so terrible in the light streaming in through the viewport that everyone fled before him. He stumbled again in the place of the machinery, and down on his hands and knees he fondled the bits of metal which he could see in the dim light through the open door. 'Where's the buzzer?' he sobbed. 'I must find the buzzer.' Crifer's voice, from the darkness inside, said, 'You broke it. You broke it. And now we will break you—' Rikud got up and ran. He reached the door again and then he slipped down against it, exhausted. Behind him, the voices and the footsteps came, and soon he saw Crifer's head peer in through the passageway. Then there were others, and then they were walking toward him. His head whirled and the viewport seemed to swim in a haze. Could it be variable, as Crifer had suggested? He wondered if the scurrying brown thing waited somewhere, and nausea struck at the pit of his stomach. But if the plants could live out there and the scurrying thing could live and that was why the world had moved through the blackness, then so could he live out there, and Crifer and all the others.... So tightly did he grip the handle that his fingers began to hurt. And his heart pounded hard and he felt the pulses leaping on either side of his neck. He stared out into the garden, and off into the distance, where the blue-white globe which might have been a star stood just above the row of mounds. Crifer was tugging at him, trying to pull him away from the door, and someone was grabbing at his legs, trying to make him fall. He kicked out and the hands let go, and then he turned the handle and shoved the weight of his body with all his strength against the door. It opened and he stepped outside into the warmth. The air was fresh, fresher than any air Rikud had ever breathed. He walked around aimlessly, touching the plants and bending down to feel the floor, and sometimes he looked at the blue-white globe on the horizon. It was all very beautiful. Near the ship, water that did not come from a machine gurgled across the land, and Rikud lay down and drank. It was cool and good, and when he got up, Crifer and Wilm were outside the world, and some of the others followed. They stood around for a long time before going to the water to drink. Rikud sat down and tore off a piece of a plant, munching on it. It was good. Crifer picked his head up, from the water, his chin wet. 'Even feelings are variable. I don't hate you now, Rikud.' Rikud smiled, staring at the ship. 'People are variable, too, Crifer. That is, if those creatures coming from the ship are people.' 'They're women,' said Crifer. They were strangely shaped in some ways, and yet in others completely human, and their voices were high, like singing. Rikud found them oddly exciting. He liked them. He liked the garden, for all its hugeness. With so many people, and especially now with women, he was not afraid. It was much better than the small world of machinery, buzzer, frightening doors and women by appointment only. Rikud felt at home.

units.evidence: Now I knew she was at the breaking point, because Val didn't lie unless she was so exhausted she didn't know what she was doing.

units.claim: Ron feels guilty for bringing Val to Mars, but remembers she volunteered first.
units.evidence: I felt almost guilty for having dragged her out to Mars, until I recalled that I hadn't. In fact, she had come up with the idea before I did.

units.claim: Ron decides to rest before continuing their journey.
units.evidence: I think we ought to rest a little before we go any further. It's been a long, hard day.

units.claim: Val falls asleep quickly after resting.
units.evidence: She slid down beside me, curled up, and in a moment she was fast asleep, sprawled out on the sands.

units.claim: Ron reflects on their decision to come to Mars.
units.evidence: Maybe we shouldn't have come to Mars after all. But, I reminded myself, someone had to do the job.

units.claim: Ron watches Val sleeping and thinks about their life on Earth.
units.evidence: I watched her, sleeping peacefully, a wayward lock of her soft blonde hair trailing down over one eyebrow, and it seemed hard to believe that we'd exchanged Earth and all it held for us for the raw, untamed struggle that was Mars.

units.claim: Ron decides not to wake Val and continues to watch the desert.
units.evidence: But then Val stirred and rolled over in her sleep, and I didn't have the heart to wake her. I sat there, holding her, staring out over the desert, watching the wind whip the sand up into weird shapes.

units.claim: Dorffman protested that they know the other party is right.
units.evidence: "But we know you're right," Dorffman protested.

units.claim: Lessing questions if they know the other party is right.
units.evidence: "Do we?"

units.claim: Dorffman asserts that they know the other party is right by pointing to their work and observations.
units.evidence: "Of course we do! Look at our work! Look at what we've seen on the Farm."

units.claim: Lessing acknowledges their work but suggests looking at Tommy Gilman quickly.
units.evidence: "Yes, I know." Lessing's voice was weary. "But first I think we'd better look at Tommy Gilman, and the quicker we look, the better—"

units.claim: A nurse informs them that they called the Farm but the doctors had already left.
units.evidence: A nurse greeted them as they stepped off the elevator. "We called you at the Farm, but you'd already left. The boy—" She broke off helplessly. "He's sick, Doctor. He's sicker than we ever imagined."

units.claim: The nurse describes the boy's condition as worse than expected.
units.evidence: She broke off helplessly. "He's sick, Doctor. He's sicker than we ever imagined."

units.claim: The nurse cannot precisely describe what happened to the boy.
units.evidence: "Nothing exactly—happened. I don't quite know how to describe it."

units.claim: The nurse leads them to a children's playroom.
units.evidence: She hurried them down the corridor and opened a door into a large children's playroom.

units.claim: Tommy sits in the corner of the room without showing recognition or pleasure.
units.evidence: The boy sat stolidly in the corner of the room. He looked up as they came in, but there was no flicker of recognition or pleasure on his pale face.

units.claim: Tommy is wearing a monitor helmet.
units.evidence: The monitor helmet was still on his head.

units.claim: Tommy grips a toy fire engine tightly.
units.evidence: He just sat there, gripping a toy fire engine tightly in his hands.

units.claim: Lessing attempts to speak to Tommy but receives no response.
units.evidence: Lessing crossed the room swiftly. "Tommy," he said. The boy didn't even look at him. He stared stupidly at the fire engine.

units.claim: Tommy reacts with fear when Lessing tries to take the toy fire engine.
units.evidence: "Tommy!" Lessing reached out for the toy. The boy drew back in terror, clutching it to his chest. "Go away," he choked. "Go away, go away—" When Lessing persisted the boy bent over swiftly and bit him hard on the hand.

units.claim: Lessing promises not to take the toy again.
units.evidence: Lessing sat down on the table. "Tommy, listen to me." His voice was gentle. "I won't try to take it again. I promise."

units.claim: Tommy continues to ask Lessing to leave.
units.evidence: "Go away."

units.claim: Tommy confirms he knows who Lessing is.
units.evidence: Tommy's eyes shifted haltingly to Lessing's face. He nodded. "Go away."

units.claim: Tommy expresses that he is in pain.
units.evidence: "Why are you afraid, Tommy?" "I hurt. My head hurts. I hurt all over. Go away."

units.claim: Tommy mentions he can't get something off.
units.evidence: "Why do you hurt?" "I—can't get it—off," the boy said.

units.claim: Lessing suspects the monitor helmet is causing the problem.
units.evidence: The monitor, Lessing thought suddenly. Something had suddenly gone horribly wrong—could the boy really be sensing the source of the trouble?

units.claim: Lessing feels a cold knot in his stomach.
units.evidence: Lessing felt a cold knot gather in the pit of his stomach.

units.claim: Lessing recalls seeing similar effects at the Farm.
units.evidence: He had seen it a hundred times at the Farm.

units.claim: Lessing realizes the boy is sick.
units.evidence: But this youngster was sick—

units.claim: Lessing decides to remove the monitor helmet.
units.evidence: With trembling fingers Lessing reached out and opened the baffle-snap on the monitor. "Take it off, Tommy," he whispered.

units.claim: Tommy removes the helmet in surprise.
units.evidence: The boy blinked in amazement, and pulled the grey helmet from his head.

units.claim: Lessing feels a familiar prickly sensation when the helmet is removed.
units.evidence: Lessing felt the familiar prickly feeling run down his scalp as the boy stared at him.

units.claim: Lessing senses the boy's terror fading.
units.evidence: He could feel deep in his own mind the cold chill of terror radiating from the boy. Then, suddenly, it began to fade.

units.claim: A sense of warmth, peace, and security replaces the fear.
units.evidence: A sense of warmth—peace and security and comfort—swept in as the fear faded from the boy's face.

units.claim: Tommy drops the toy fire engine.
units.evidence: The fire engine clattered to the floor.

units.claim: They analyze the tapes and data cards later.
units.evidence: They analyzed the tapes later, punching the data cards with greatest care, filing them through the machines for the basic processing and classification that all their data underwent.

units.claim: Dorffman believes the data is incorrect and does not fit previous observations.
units.evidence: Dorffman stared at it angrily. "It's obviously wrong," he grated. "It doesn't fit. Dave, it doesn't agree with anything we've observed before. There must be an error."

units.claim: Lessing points out that the theory predicts adult psi-contact is harmful to children.
units.evidence: "Of course," said Lessing. "According to the theory. The theory says that adult psi-contact is deadly to the growing child. It smothers their potential through repeated contact until it dries up completely. We've proved that, haven't we? Time after time. Everything goes according to the theory—except Tommy. But Tommy's psi-potential was drying up there on the Farm, until the distortion was threatening the balance of his mind. Then he made an adult contact, and we saw how he bloomed."

units.claim: Lessing feels they need to formulate a new theory for Tommy.
units.evidence: Lessing sank down to his desk wearily. "What are we going to do, Jack? Formulate a separate theory for Tommy?"

units.claim: Dorffman believes the instruments were wrong.
units.evidence: "Of course not," said Dorffman. "The instruments were wrong. Somehow we misread the data—"

units.claim: Lessing argues that the boy's behavior and appearance indicate something different happened.
units.evidence: "Didn't you see his face?" Lessing burst out. "Didn't you see how he acted? What do you want with an instrument reading?" He shook his head. "It's no good, Jack. Something different happened here, something we'd never counted on. It's something the theory just doesn't allow for."

units.claim: Lessing considers revising their book and presentation.
units.evidence: Lessing said slowly. "It'll be costly—but it might even be fun. It's a pretty dry, logical presentation of ideas, as it stands. Very austere and authoritarian. But a few revisions could change all that—" He rubbed his hands together thoughtfully.

units.claim: Lessing wonders if they have the courage to face ridicule and discredit.
units.evidence: "How about it, Jack? Do we have nerve enough to be laughed at? Do you think we could stand a little discredit, making silly asses of ourselves? Because when I finish this book, we'll be laughed out of existence. There won't be any Authority in psionics for a while—and maybe that way one of the lads who's really sniffing out the trail will get somebody to listen to him!"

units.claim: Lessing plans to send a copy of their revised work to someone in Chicago.
units.evidence: "Get a pad, get a pencil! We've got work to do. And when we finish, I think we'll send a carbon copy out Chicago way. Might even persuade that puppy out there to come here and work for me—"

units.claim: The judge muttered about needing the oath.
units.evidence: "The oath," muttered the judge. "We've got to have the oath."

units.claim: Four natives carried huge inscribed marble slabs to the front of the court.
units.evidence: The prosecutor nodded, and four natives moved forward, carrying huge inscribed marble slabs to the front of the court.

units.claim: The witness placed a paw on the pile of marble slabs.
units.evidence: The witness placed a huge, hairy paw on the cairn

units.claim: The prosecutor asked the witness to swear to tell the truth.
units.evidence: "Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help you—"

units.claim: The prosecutor was unsure of the ending of the oath.
units.evidence: he paused to squint at the paper in his hand, and finished on a puzzled note, "—Goddess?"

units.claim: The witness scratched his ear and replied 'Of course' in an injured tone.
units.evidence: The witness removed the paw from the rock pile long enough to scratch his ear. Then he replaced it, and replied, "Of course," in an injured tone.

units.claim: The witness was asked to tell the court what he had seen of the defendant's activities.
units.evidence: "Then tell this court what you have seen of the activities of this abominable wretch."

units.claim: The witness was uncertain about the exact date of the event.
units.evidence: I think it happened on the fourth night of the seventh crossing of Altair II (may the Goddess cast a drought upon it)—or was it the seventh night of the fourth crossing?

units.claim: The witness was returning through town towards his land-plot after weeks of bargaining for the crop he was harvesting.
units.evidence: when I was making my way back through town toward my blessed land-plot, minding my own business, Your Honor, after weeks of bargaining for the crop I was harvesting.

units.claim: Zeckler objected to the witness's testimony due to the witness's uncertainty about the date.
units.evidence: "Objection!" Zeckler squealed plaintively, jumping to his feet. "This witness can't even remember what night he's talking about!"

units.claim: The judge overruled Zeckler's objection.
units.evidence: The judge looked startled. Then he pawed feverishly through his bundle of notes. "Overruled," he said abruptly. "Continue, please."

units.claim: The witness described Zeckler as a desperate criminal type.
units.evidence: I could see that I was face to face with the most desperate of criminal types, even for Terrans.

units.claim: Zeckler claimed he had never seen the witness before.
units.evidence: "I never saw him before in my life," Zeckler moaned to Meyerhoff.

units.claim: Meyerhoff explained that the Goddess controls the weather on the planet.
units.evidence: Meyerhoff gave him a stony look. "The Goddess runs things around here. She makes it rain. If it doesn't rain, somebody's insulted her. It's very simple."

units.claim: Zeckler expressed concern about fighting the testimony.
units.evidence: "But how can I fight testimony like that?"

units.claim: Meyerhoff doubted Zeckler's ability to fight the testimony.
units.evidence: "I doubt if you can fight it."

units.claim: Another witness testified about the slaughter of eighteen or twenty-three women and children.
units.evidence: This one was testifying regarding the butcherous slaughter of eighteen (or was it twenty-three? Oh, yes, twenty-three) women and children in the suburban village of Karzan.

units.claim: Zeckler felt increasingly desperate as the testimony continued.
units.evidence: Zeckler grew paler and paler, his eyes turning glassy as the testimony piled up.

units.claim: Zeckler whispered to Meyerhoff that the testimony was not true.
units.evidence: "But it's not true," he whispered to Meyerhoff.

units.claim: Meyerhoff stated that the people did not value truth.
units.evidence: These people have no regard for truth. It's stupid, to them, silly, a mark of low intelligence.

units.claim: Zeckler stood up to make a statement before the verdict.
units.evidence: Zeckler jerked around abruptly as he heard his name bellowed out. "Does the defendant have anything to say before the jury delivers the verdict?"

units.claim: Zeckler claimed his statement would be important for the case.
units.evidence: Your—Your Honor, I—I have a statement to make which will have a most important bearing on this case.

units.claim: Zeckler warned the judge and others about a grave danger.
units.evidence: You are in gravest of danger. All of you. Your lives—your very land is at stake.

units.claim: Zeckler admitted that the charges against him seemed true.
units.evidence: These charges, all of them—they're perfectly true. At least, they seem to be perfectly true.

units.claim: Zeckler claimed he was working for the welfare of the planet.
units.evidence: But in every instance, I was working with heart and soul, risking my life, for the welfare of your beautiful planet.

units.claim: Zeckler mentioned a conspiracy involving the Goddess.
units.evidence: Because in attempting to arrange trading in that frightful place, I made certain contacts. I learned the horrible thing which is about to happen to this planet, at the hands of those barbarians. The conspiracy is theirs, not mine. They have bribed your Goddess, flattered her and lied to her, coerced her all-powerful goodness to their own evil interests, preparing for the day when they could persuade her to cast your land into the fiery furnace of a ten-year-drought—

units.claim: The court laughed at Zeckler's statement about bribing the Goddess.
units.evidence: Somebody in the middle of the court burst out laughing. One by one the natives nudged one another, and booed, and guffawed, until the rising tide of racket drowned out Zeckler's words.

units.claim: The prosecutor claimed the defendant was lying about the Goddess being bribed.
units.evidence: The defendant is obviously lying," roared the prosecutor over the pandemonium. "Any fool knows that the Goddess can't be bribed. How could she be a Goddess if she could?
